subject: ddply() drops a number of subsets with large data

messages.author: 71171f0d61fc140f
messages.subject: ddply() drops a number of subsets with large data
parts:
Hi all,

I've come across a nasty bug, and I'm not sure of its source. Also,
unfortunately, I'm unable to share the data set where the bug is
cropping up. Hopefully my code will be clear though.

###############
## speaker.id is the column names of a number of id variables

dput(speaker.id)
#c("Name", "Age", "Sex", "Ethnicity", "Education", "Street", "Year",
#"File", "DOB")

## Step 1: Simply split speaker level data into a list.
data.l <- dlply(all_philly, speaker.id, function(x)x)

## Step 2: For each level of VClass within a speaker's data,
## calculate the mean of value, return as a list.
means1.l <- llply(data.l, function(x){
ddply(x, .(VClass), summarise, value = mean(value))
}, .progress = "text")

## Step 3, simply recombine the means from the list into a data frame
means1.df <- ldply(means1.l, function(x)x)

## For comparison, combine the above three steps into one with ddply
means2.df <- ddply(all_philly, c(speaker.id, "VClass"), summarise,
value = mean(value))

## Count up simply how many VClass categories there are per speaker.
a <- ddply(means1.df, .(Name), nrow)
b <- ddply(means2.df, .(Name), nrow)

## Compare
error <- merge(a, b, by = "Name")

table(error$V1.x == error$V1.y)
#FALSE TRUE
# 133 122

## The first 122 speakers in alphabetical order are fine
summary( (error$V1.y / error$V1.x)[1:122])
# Min. 1st Qu. Median Mean 3rd Qu. Max.
# 1 1 1 1 1 1

## Speakers 123 through 255 have only about a quarter of the
## means that they ought to
summary( (error$V1.y / error$V1.x)[123:155])
# Min. 1st Qu. Median Mean 3rd Qu. Max.
# 0.2500 0.2759 0.2759 0.2782 0.2857 0.2963
###################

So after the 122nd speaker, the simple ddply call starts dropping
about three quarters of the subsets.This seems like a pretty bad bug,
and I didn't realize it was happening for a while.

I should note that there is nothing, in principle, special about the
data from speakers 123 through 125 in alphabetical order. The
speaker's name in the data is not systematically correlated with
anything related to their time of collection, or addition to the data
set.

Here's my session info.

-Joe

messages.author: 71171f0d61fc140f
messages.subject: Re: ddply() drops a number of subsets with large data
parts:
I'm chasing a hunch that the bug is caused by the number of possible subsets defined by the data structure. I have 10 columns, which if all of their levels were fully crossed would lead to 

max(cumprod(apply(fake.data[,1:10], 2, max)))
[1] 1.880338e+16

Possible subsets. But, there are actually only 7,730 actual subsets in the data.

If I paste together the values from these 10 columns into one ID column, the bug goes away.

#########
speaker.id <- c("Name", "Age", "Sex", "Ethnicity", "Education",  "Street", "File", "DOB", "Year")
fake.data$ID <- with(fake.data, paste(
             Name, Age,  Sex, Ethnicity, Education, Street, Year, File, DOB, VClass,
             sep = "_"))
length(unique(fake.data$ID))
## [1] 7730

means3.df <- ddply(fake.data, .(ID), summarise, value = mean(value), .progress = "text")
nrow(means3.df)
## [1] 7730

means4.df <- ddply(fake.data, c(speaker.id, "VClass"), summarise, value = mean(value), .progress = "text")
nrow(means4.df)
## [1] 4776
#########

If I drop Sex, which has two levels, halving the number of possible subsets, the bug is mitigated.

#########
speaker.id2 <- c("Name", "Age", "Ethnicity", "Education",  "Street", "File", "DOB", "Year")
means5.df <- ddply(fake.data, c(speaker.id2, "VClass"), summarise, value = mean(value), .progress = "text")
nrow(means5.df)
## [1] 7482
#########

After Sex, the factor with the fewest unique values is Education, which has 20. Dropping education, or any one of the remaining factors eliminates the bug altogether.

-Joe

parts:
Ah, it's related to this bug: https://github.com/hadley/plyr/issues/63

The development version at least throws an error in this circumstance,
but I need to figure out an alternative implementation of the strategy
that works for larger datasets.

Hadley
